Figure 2 instead draws a dashed vertical drop from (cos x, sin x) to the base and omits the chord, so the main small-triangle topology is wrong; it also makes the tangent height dashed rather than a solid triangle edge and places the side-by-side area labels less accurately under the extracted shapes.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1 is slightly better because its angle slider and overlay toggle recompute the same geometry as Figure 2 but the overlay handler also hides and restores redundant dashed arc artifacts, so the advertised overlaid comparison remains clearer and more coherent. Figure 2’s basic controls also work, but its overlay leaves extra dashed geometry/annotation clutter and its panel labels are less consistently aligned with the regions they control; both figures share the same limitation that the angle slider is narrowed to 0.1–1.4 rather than the requested 0 to π/2 and becomes unwieldy near the upper end.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is recognizable as the original unit-circle and sector/triangle inequality diagram, with the same blue circle/arcs, red triangle outlines, labels, and three comparison panels, while Figure 2 does not render the figure at all and only shows an error message.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 includes most of the original mathematical labels and annotations, such as the point labels, x angle labels, area captions, inequalities, and fraction formulas, though many are quite small at inline size and some annotations are less readable than the reference. concept.rationale: Figure 1 more accurately represents the proof geometry because its left unit-circle diagram includes the chord from (cos x, sin x) to (1, 0), so the inner triangle with base 1 and altitude sin x corresponds to the stated area sin x/2 and the inequality tan x/2 >= x/2 >= sin x/2 (L00010). Figure 2 instead draws a vertical drop from (cos x, sin x) to the x-axis and omits the chord on the left, visually suggesting a different right triangle of area sin x cos x/2 rather than the triangle used for the sandwiching argument, even though its right-side extracted triangle and labels are mostly correct (L00010).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is clearly stronger: it renders the intended unit-circle squeeze-theorem diagram with the chord from (cos x, sin x) to (1, 0), solid tangent-triangle boundary, comparison panels, and most mathematical labels intact. Figure 2 is much weaker because in the rendered view it only shows an error message, and even at the source-code level it omits the key chord and substitutes a misleading vertical drop that suggests the wrong inner triangle area. Figure 1 also has slightly cleaner interactive overlay behavior, whereas Figure 2 leaves extra dashed clutter and less well-aligned panel annotations.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better preserves the intended two-plane transformation structure: its axes have properly centered arrowheads, the mapped boundary curves are explicitly drawn as unfilled stroked paths, and labels are anchored more consistently to the corresponding curves and axes. Figure 2 has the same basic topology, but its arrowheads are less accurately constructed, its text styling/positioning is less reliable, and its mapped extended curves are drawn as polylines without an explicit fill suppression, which risks unintended filled shapes and weaker structural fidelity.

interactivity.rationale: Both figures correctly bind the x(u,v) and y(u,v) equation fields so valid edits recompute and redraw the mapped region while invalid expressions show errors and keep the last valid drawing, but Figure 1 handles the corner-drag interaction more correctly: dragging the (u₀,v₀) corner moves the rectangle with fixed side lengths as its tooltip/description indicates, while Figure 2 instead resizes the rectangle from that corner despite advertising it as a move control. Figure 1 also keeps the dragged rectangle consistently constrained within the intended uv-panel area, whereas Figure 2 permits more awkward placements relative to the drawn axes.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more visually faithful because it preserves the two-panel composition, cyan rectangle in the uv-plane, beige transformation arrow, and a recognizable curved quadrilateral image region with blue boundary curves and labels. Figure 2 has a somewhat similar left rectangle, but the mapped region is rendered as dark black distorted shapes rather than the light-blue curved patch of the original, making the right half read as a different figure.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 has more of the required textbook labels, including S, R, both u-boundary image labels, and attempts at both v-image labels, whereas Figure 2 omits or effectively loses important labels such as R and the image of v = v0 + Δv. concept.rationale: Figure 1 is more conceptually accurate because its default rectangle has a smaller Δv and produces an image that better matches the intended “slightly distorted parallelogram”/curved quadrilateral for a not-too-large parameter rectangle (L00007, L00010), while Figure 2’s larger default parameter region under the same polar-type map gives a more strongly curved annular sector that is less faithful to the local-change-of-variables picture. Both correctly show S bounded by constant u and v lines with Δu, Δv labels and map the four sides to labeled image curves (L00010), but Figure 1 better supports the small-region Jacobian motivation than Figure 2.

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is stronger across all dimensions: it preserves the intended two-panel transformation with a cyan uv-rectangle, beige mapping arrow, labeled source/image regions, and a light-blue curved quadrilateral image, while Figure 2’s right-hand image appears as darker distorted shapes with missing or illegible labels. In the source-level behavior, Figure 1 also implements the advertised corner-drag movement and panel constraints more correctly, whereas Figure 2 resizes from the corner despite describing a move control and has less reliable arrowhead, curve, and label construction. Conceptually, Figure 1’s smaller default region better supports the local change-of-variables/Jacobian picture, while Figure 2’s larger mapped sector looks less like the intended slightly distorted parallelogram.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better preserves the textbook-style structure: the main curve is partitioned cleanly, the selected sub-arc is highlighted with proper endpoint labels, the Δs_k dimension arcs include arrowheads and perpendicular boundary extension lines, and the inset segment/formula layout is clearer. Figure 1’s sliders do redraw and its Riemann-sum value updates, but the zoom inset is a fixed generic curve independent of the selected partition segment, so the n control changes the highlighted arc on the main curve while the isolated kth arc does not actually update to match it; both also use a slider rather than true dragging and neither shows sample points multiplying along every segment.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is much more recognizable as the reference: it preserves the main left curve with loop, the beige arrow pointing to the smaller arc on the right, the boxed formula near the bottom, and the overall composition and blue/cream color scheme. Figure 2 does have minor notation/label-rendering weaknesses, such as some non-k partition labels and baseline asterisks, but these are less damaging than Figure 1’s mismatch between the highlighted arc and the isolated arc.

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is the stronger overall choice because it much more faithfully matches the reference composition, curve shape, color scheme, label structure, endpoint annotations, Δs_k markings, and formula placement, whereas Figure 2 distorts the layout with misplaced or garbled labels, a broad wavy arrow, and less complete dimension annotation. Figure 2 has an advantage in tying its inset more directly to the highlighted kth segment in the code, but that conceptual/interactivity strength is outweighed by Figure 1’s clearer geometry and much higher rendered faithfulness and label quality.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better matches the likely textbook geometry of a localized surface patch with a translated fluid volume, visible/hidden boundary edges, leader arrows, and a callout integrated into the scene. interactivity.rationale: Figure 2 implements a working patch-position control that recomputes the patch geometry on the full surface, moves the labels/leaders, and reorients the normal consistently as the patch moves, while Figure 1 has no patch-location interaction at all and its normal never reorients. Both figures have a flow-velocity slider that redraws an extruded volume and arrows proportionally, but Figure 2's slider is integrated with the movable patch, whereas Figure 1 only changes the height of a fixed patch and even accumulates stale interactive registrations on each redraw. Figure 2 is not perfect because the patch is moved by a one-dimensional slider rather than true dragging and it does not numerically update ΔS_k, but its controls much more closely match the intended interactions.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more recognizable as the textbook figure because it preserves the main turquoise curved surface patch, the upward normal arrow, surface/area labels, and a beige callout/arrow element in roughly the same conceptual composition. concept.rationale: Figure 2 is conceptually more accurate because it keeps the normal vector independent of flow speed and makes it perpendicular to the curved surface patch, which better represents the unit normal used in the flux factor F(x*_k,y*_k,z*_k)·n(x*_k,y*_k,z*_k)ΔS_k (L00021-L00027, L00057). Figure 1 does show a teal patch, upward normal, flow arrows, and the caption idea, but it incorrectly scales the displayed normal length with the flow-velocity slider even though n is a unit normal, which can teach a false dependence of n on |v| (L00014-L00019, L00057). Figure 2 also better preserves the distinction between vertical flow and the normal component through a sloped patch, whereas Figure 1 effectively collapses the example to the special case where flow and the central normal are aligned, making the dot-product idea less generally truthful (L00015-L00027, L00053-L00057).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is the stronger overall match because it more faithfully preserves the localized turquoise surface patch, upward normal, area/surface labels, leader arrows, and callout composition, with annotations that remain more legible and better connected to the depicted geometry. faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 and Figure 2 appear visually indistinguishable: both show the same single-panel H2 adsorption view with the same green Ni surface, white hydrogen atoms, labels, camera angle, scale, and side reaction-phase control, so neither is more faithful than the other.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 and Figure 2 are indistinguishable in source and therefore equally accurate: both depict the same Ni-surface hydrogenation sequence with H adsorption/H–H cleavage, ethylene adsorption with π-bond loss/Ni–C interaction, H migration to form C–H bonds, and ethane desorption, matching the core mechanism described in the caption and authored brief (L00007, L00012, L00018-L00019). They also share the same limitations, such as representing Ni–H bonding only implicitly through surface H atoms rather than explicitly, so neither is conceptually better than the other (L00018).

concept.rationale: Figure 1 is more conceptually accurate because it includes the arctan activation annotation associated with the generator's fractional convolution pipeline, whereas Figure 2 omits arctan entirely despite the brief specifying fractional/transposed convolutions with arctan activations (L00007). concept.rationale: Figure 1 is more conceptually accurate overall because its main network flow more faithfully asserts the requested staged tensor dimensions, separate MaxPool, subsampling transitions, and simultaneous repeated-block annotations such as 24 and 36 blocks total (L00007). Figure 2 has the same serious inset error as Figure 1—both show a BN/ReLU/Conv pre-activation order rather than the specified Conv 1x1, BN, ReLU, Conv 3x3, BN, ReLU, Conv 1x1 sequence (L00007)—but Figure 2 additionally misrepresents the macro architecture by not clearly drawing the MaxPool between the 7x7 convolution and residual stages and by making the 24/36 block count a Stage 3 slider rather than showing the fixed repeated-stage annotations described in the brief (L00007). Although Figure 1 has cramped labels and some conceptual issues in the residual inset and channel counts, these are minor relative to Figure 2’s nonfunctional error state and less faithful architecture reconstruction.
